note: Residents of the town of Kakunya asked Rav Yosef to send someone to set up an eiruv for their town. He sent Abaye, warning him to make sure there would be no outcry against it in the study hall. Abaye saw some houses that opened onto the river rather than the town and decided they could be the part left outside the eiruv. Then he changed his mind again and again: such houses do not qualify, so he would cut windows to link them; windows are unnecessary, as Rabba bar Avuh's eiruv in Meḥoza shows; that case is different, so windows are needed; and finally, windows are not needed, since a straw storehouse in Pumbedita once served as the part left out.
why: The mishna says a public city that became private may not have one eiruv for all of it unless a section is left out. Abaye's reversals show how hard that rule is to apply, and afterward he grasps Rav Yosef's warning.

note: Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua went and told Rava of Abaye's ruling that Jews sharing an alleyway with a gentile could all give up their rights to one of them, who could then carry there. Rava objected that this would abolish the eiruv in that alleyway. Rav Huna answered that they could still make an eiruv as a reminder; Rava said people would then think an eiruv works even where a gentile lives. Rav Huna said they would make an announcement; Rava retorted: will you make an announcement for the children?
why: Abaye has just told the Jewish neighbors of a gentile to give up their rights in the alleyway to one person; this exchange rejects that solution, and Rava then offers his own: borrowing a place from the gentile.

note: A baby's warm water for his Shabbat circumcision had spilled, and Rava offered to give up his rights to his own courtyard so water could be carried over from it. Ravina challenged him: didn't Shmuel say rights cannot be given up from one courtyard to another? Rava said he followed Rabbi Yoḥanan on that. Ravina asked why, then, Rava did not stay where he was, give up his rights, and have the others give theirs back to him afterward, as Rav allows. Rava said that on this he followed Shmuel, who forbids it. Ravina pressed that both rulings rest on one reason; Rava answered that Shmuel's reason here is different: so that the Sages' rules do not become a joke.
why: The Gemara has been telling of spilled circumcision water on Shabbat; Rava's plan leads into the question whether rights can be given up and given back, which the Gemara then takes up as a dispute between Rav and Shmuel.

note: Ulla was staying at the house of Rav Menashe on Shabbat when a man came and knocked on the door. Ulla said: Who is that? May his body be desecrated, since he desecrates Shabbat. Rabba told him the Sages forbade only musical sounds on Shabbat, not knocking. Abaye raised an objection to Rabba from a teaching that allows drawing wine with a siphon and dripping water for a sick person on Shabbat; the answer does not come within the story.
why: After the mishna's ruling on drawing water from the Cistern of the Exiles on Shabbat, the Gemara turns to whether making a sound on Shabbat is forbidden; Ulla's curse and Rabba's reply open that debate.
